claims.text: High-temperature gas-exposure degradation is governed by a surface-mediated selective-oxidation mechanism involving Cr and Ti.
Selective oxidation of Cr and Ti produces a nonuniform, defect-prone oxide scale.
In an oxidizing atmosphere, the oxide scale is initially thin and protective.
In an oxidizing atmosphere, compositional inhomogeneity and thermal stresses eventually cause oxide-scale cracking and spallation.
In a reducing atmosphere, partial reduction of the scale generates porosity.
Porosity generated by scale reduction permits deeper gas penetration and accelerates subsurface or internal oxidation and weakening.
The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy initially has a single-phase FCC matrix.
The constituent elements are relatively homogeneous in the initial alloy.
Elevated-temperature diffusion and surface segregation cause preferential oxidation of Cr and Ti.
Cr can contribute to protective passivation or oxidation resistance in compositionally complex alloys.
Both the oxidizing-atmosphere and reducing-atmosphere pathways compromise the alloy's mechanical integrity.
After high-temperature exposure, strength and fatigue resistance will be reduced relative to the as-manufactured state.
Oxidizing exposure will produce a relatively thick, uneven oxide scale exhibiting cracking or spallation.
Reducing exposure will produce a thinner but more porous and discontinuous oxide scale.
Both exposure conditions will cause measurable near-surface depletion of Cr and Ti.
The proposed mechanism applies over 800–1200 °C in either oxygen-rich or low-oxygen reducing atmospheres.
At lower temperatures, oxidation kinetics may be too slow for the proposed mechanism to govern degradation.
Al may also contribute to oxidation behavior, although its exact role is uncertain.
Additive-manufacturing residual porosity or residual stress may affect the degradation mechanism.
Exposure at 1000 °C for 50 hours in pure O2 versus 5% H2 in N2, followed by microscopy, compositional profiling, and mechanical testing, provides a controlled comparison of the proposed pathways.
